title: Three times a day
hookLine: the Didache's rhythm: the Lord's Prayer morning, noon and night
tomorrow: what if reading less of the Bible is the point?

lines: UP TO THE ROOF TO PRAY.
cards: A stomach growls at midday, somewhere between one class or meeting and the next. In Acts, Peter's does too. He's staying in Joppa, in a house by the sea.

Downstairs someone is getting a meal ready, and Acts says “he became very hungry.” Instead of hovering by the kitchen, he climbs to the flat roof: he “went up upon the housetop to pray about the sixth hour.”
Hot sun, the smell of cooking drifting up, and a set hour that took him upstairs.

teach.h: THE HOUR OF PRAYER, THE NINTH HOUR.
teach.b: Acts shows another set hour: “Peter and John went up together into the temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour.” The first believers kept hours of prayer they already knew.

teach.h: THE DIDACHE: THREE TIMES A DAY.
teach.b: And an early Christian handbook, the Didache, gives its own rhythm: pray the Lord's Prayer three times a day. It doesn't name the hours; it gives the prayer and the number.
So why fixed times, when Paul says “Pray without ceasing”? Because a habit needs hooks. Three stops are how a day learns to pray always.

teach.h: A SOUND THAT CALLS THE HOUR.
teach.b: Set hours have often been carried by sound. In some churches a bell still rings at morning, noon and evening for a prayer called the Angelus.
A bell, the height of the sun, the smell of a meal: the body knows the hour before the mind decides. Today an alarm can do the same work.
And the sound comes on days nobody feels like praying, with the same short prayer waiting.

Look at Peter's hour again: hungry, hot, dinner not ready. He prays anyway, and Acts says that's when the vision comes, a great sheet let down from heaven. An ordinary midday became the hour something new opened.

how: Some Christians pray the Lord's Prayer or a short set prayer at fixed times each day, and some churches ring a bell at morning, noon and evening as a call to pray.

games.q: what does “three times a day” mean?
o: eating three meals a day as a spiritual discipline
going to church services three days each week
praying the Lord's Prayer at morning, noon and night

games.q: set hours in Acts — tap the pairs.
p: Peter and John at the temple
the Lord's Prayer three times a day

s: the Didache names the exact hours for prayer
it gives the prayer and the number, and doesn't name the hours.
praying at fixed times means you pray only three times
the stops are hooks; Paul's hope is pray without ceasing.
Peter went up to pray while the meal was still being made
he became very hungry, and went up anyway.

games.q: your midday reminder goes off in a loud, crowded cafeteria. what fits the lesson?
o: skip it; set hours only work somewhere quiet.
the short prayer, or one breath, right where you are.
move it to a time when you're always alone.
games.why: Peter's hour came on a roof, hungry, with dinner cooking. the set time finds you where you are, and the prayer is short enough to fit.

practice: Pick up your phone and set three quiet reminders: waking, midday, lying down. Choose one sound for all three, play it once now, and listen to it all the way to silence.
If you pray, let that sound mean the Lord's Prayer; if not, let it mean one slow breath and a moment of attention.

wordCard.voice: Three times a day. The Didache's rhythm: the Lord's Prayer, said at set stops through the day.

orig.note: the Didache's Greek: three times a day.

carryVoice: Keep this: morning, noon, night, three stops and one short prayer. Until the next one.
